strengths: The paper addresses a practically important NLP problem: forecasting later validation loss to select hyperparameters directly on the target model. Token-position decomposition provides an interpretable perspective on pretraining dynamics.

Experiments cover 468M and 1.2B models trained for 400B tokens, ID and OOD validation datasets, and several forecasting cutoffs. The reported hyperbolic fits and prefix-based forecasts provide promising empirical evidence beyond full-trajectory curve fitting.

The mixture-selection application evaluates completed training runs, reporting lower perplexity in all four model/dataset settings and improved benchmark accuracy in 12 of 14 comparisons. The appendices provide useful architecture, software, and weighting-strategy details.
weaknesses: The central baseline comparison requires correction or explanation. Table 1 reports strongly negative in-sample R² for a power law fitted to the complete trajectory. The stated family L=(p1x)^p2+p3 contains a constant predictor when p2=0, so its optimal least-squares fit cannot perform worse than predicting the mean, absent unreported constraints. These results suggest fitting or evaluation problems rather than establishing that power laws fail. This unresolved issue materially undermines the superiority claim and prevents a sound Findings recommendation.

An essential ablation is missing. After a0 and a1 are fixed at Nsep, Eq. (10) reduces to a constant plus the cosine-based a2 term. The proposed method explicitly exploits the known learning-rate schedule, whereas the baselines do not. Fitting an equivalent schedule-dependent piecewise model directly to aggregate loss is necessary to establish the benefit of token-position decomposition.

The forecasting evaluation does not clearly separate discovery from testing: functional forms and the separation criterion are motivated using complete trajectories subsequently used for forecast evaluation. Independent runs evaluated with a frozen procedure would strengthen the evidence. Generality is also limited by using two related model configurations, one training corpus, 1024-token contexts, and one schedule; OOD evaluation text does not establish robustness across training regimes.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence remains preliminary. ID perplexity improvements are only 0.05–0.07, without uncertainty estimates; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish variation across independent training runs. Selection uses 10B tokens, or 2.5% of training, whereas Figure 3 starts at 10%. Prediction errors and final candidate rankings at the actual selection budget, together with total search cost, are needed to substantiate reliable and efficient selection.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the configuration tables. The manuscript does not provide fitting code or loss traces and omits solver initialization and constraints, outlier-filtering thresholds, checkpoint cadence, actual mixture candidates, search size, and the 58M search-model training budget. These details directly affect the central nonlinear fits and selection experiment.

Loss and perplexity reporting needs reconciliation. Applying Eq. (10) to Figure 1's fitted parameters and exponentiating gives approximately 6.97 and 6.17 for ID perplexity, whereas Table 4 reports 8.62 and 7.52 for default training under apparently the same setup. Any differences in aggregation, validation data, or checkpoints should be explicit.

The interpretation of uniform learning is stronger than the evidence supports. Eq. (17) follows from manually freezing a0 and a1. Figure 6 supports approximately uniform loss decreases, but this does not establish optimality of uniform token weights. Three suppression strategies with nearly equal results support a limited empirical negative finding, not a general conclusion that position-based weighting is unnecessary.

The novelty framing is overstated: Kaplan et al. (2020) already model loss as a function of optimization steps. The contribution should be positioned more precisely around token-position modeling and forecasting under a finite cosine schedule.
